Computer Science Labs

Image Processing · Lab 06 · Material

Noise and Denoising

MaterialPracticeQuiz

Learn to describe an image disturbance before choosing how to reduce it. A detailed drawn desk gives you a known clean reference and small features worth preserving.

What you will learn

  • Simulate repeatable Gaussian and impulse disturbances with safe arithmetic.
  • Compare linear, median and bilateral filtering on the same inputs.
  • Explain border assumptions and the tradeoff between noise and detail.
  • Measure known-reference error without claiming downstream classifier improvement.

Before this lab: Know RGB arrays, uint8 ranges, floating arithmetic and basic image display.

In this lab

  1. Additive Gaussian disturbance
  2. Impulse noise changes selected pixels
  3. A normalized local averaging kernel
  4. Gaussian scale and detail loss
  5. Median filtering for isolated extremes
  6. Bilateral filtering uses value similarity
  7. Border rules supply missing neighbors
  8. Known-reference error is a limited metric

Prepare your notebook

Use a Python notebook with OpenCV, Pillow, NumPy and Matplotlib. Run the setup once, then run the guided blocks in order. The copy button selects only the code.

The examples were checked with OpenCV 4.13, Pillow 12.3, NumPy 2.2 and Matplotlib 3.11. The repository’s Python requirements list the versions. These pages and images open offline; running the code requires the Python libraries.

Run setup once, then the teaching tasks in order. Each practice or coding-quiz solution must also run after setup alone. Images are locally drawn examples, not photographs.

Python · shared setup
import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from PIL import Image, ImageDraw
cv2.setNumThreads(1)
rng = np.random.default_rng(206)
# Draw a textured desk with printed detail; all returned arrays are RGB uint8.
def draw_scene(seed=1, kind='both'):
    generator = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    h, w = 128, 160
    yy, xx = np.mgrid[:h, :w]
    grain = 4 * np.sin(yy * 0.8 + xx * 0.04) + generator.normal(0, 1.2, (h, w))
    base = 145 + 22 * xx / w + grain
    rgb = np.stack([base + 18, base + 2, base - 15], axis=-1)
    canvas = Image.fromarray(np.clip(np.rint(rgb), 0, 255).astype('uint8'))
    draw = ImageDraw.Draw(canvas)
    if kind in ('both', 'book'):
        draw.rectangle((10, 17, 72, 98), fill=(35, 64, 105), outline=(15, 30, 52), width=2)
        draw.rectangle((10, 17, 18, 98), fill=(23, 42, 69))
        draw.text((24, 25), 'NOTES', fill=(240, 232, 201))
        for y in range(49, 85, 5):
            draw.line((25, y, 62, y), fill=(94, 128, 153), width=1)
        for y in range(90, 97, 2):
            draw.line((20, y, 70, y), fill=(221, 217, 190), width=1)
    if kind in ('both', 'mug'):
        draw.ellipse((117, 48, 149, 84), outline=(235, 229, 205), width=6)
        draw.rounded_rectangle((89, 39, 127, 100), radius=7, fill=(223, 219, 199), outline=(116, 111, 97), width=2)
        draw.ellipse((89, 32, 127, 49), fill=(243, 235, 205), outline=(83, 73, 58), width=2)
        draw.ellipse((94, 36, 122, 45), fill=(73, 45, 29))
        draw.line((96, 55, 96, 90), fill=(247, 244, 227), width=2)
        draw.text((101, 68), 'TEA', fill=(76, 103, 111))
    draw.rectangle((77, 105, 152, 124), fill=(237, 215, 119), outline=(148, 119, 62))
    draw.text((82, 109), 'tea 4pm', fill=(50, 47, 34))
    return np.asarray(canvas).copy()
clean_rgb = draw_scene(1)

The image comparisons below come from the guided code. Use their captions and shared display scales to compare each change.

Guided task 01

Additive Gaussian disturbance

Gaussian noise is modeled here as an independent random offset added to every channel value. Its mean is zero and its standard deviation is fifteen in the image’s zero-to-255 scale. That describes the unbounded sampled offsets, not the final difference after clipping. Pixels near the range limits cannot retain arbitrarily large positive or negative offsets, so clipping changes the resulting distribution.

Convert the reference to floating point before addition. Direct unsigned arithmetic can wrap or hide negative changes, producing a different disturbance from the stated model. Round and clip before returning to uint8, and keep the original reference unchanged. A local random generator with a recorded seed makes the corrupted image replayable. It does not establish that actual camera noise follows this model: real acquisition can have signal-dependent, spatial or compression effects. The difference panel is a mean absolute channel change at each pixel, displayed as an error map rather than as a photograph. Its scale is in channel-value units, not probabilities.

Try it

  1. Generate a seeded zero-mean Gaussian offset array with standard deviation fifteen.
  2. Add in floating point, then round, clip and cast to uint8.
  3. Compare the reference, corrupted image and absolute difference map.
Python · run in order
noise = np.random.default_rng(610).normal(0, 15, clean_rgb.shape)
gaussian_rgb = np.clip(np.rint(clean_rgb.astype('float32') + noise), 0, 255).astype('uint8')
difference = np.abs(gaussian_rgb.astype('float32') - clean_rgb.astype('float32')).mean(axis=2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(clean_rgb)
axes[0].set_title('Clean drawn desk')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(gaussian_rgb)
axes[1].set_title('Gaussian disturbance')
axes[1].axis('off')
error_image = axes[2].imshow(difference, cmap='magma', vmin=0, vmax=45)
axes[2].set_title('Mean absolute change')
axes[2].axis('off')
fig.colorbar(error_image, ax=axes[2], label='Mean absolute channel difference')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Inspect both broad surfaces and printed detail. The generated difference can vary across pixels even though every sampled offset uses the same stated standard deviation.

Change and compare

  • Repeat with the same local seed and verify identical corrupted pixels.
  • Halve the standard deviation while keeping the clean reference fixed.

Guided task 02

Impulse noise changes selected pixels

Impulse noise is a different disturbance: selected pixels are replaced by extreme values rather than receiving small additive changes everywhere. In this task one random number per spatial pixel determines whether all three RGB channels become black, become white, or remain unchanged. Sharing the decision across channels produces neutral black and white impulses rather than unrelated colored channel specks.

The probability intervals are disjoint. Values below 0.02 become black; values from 0.02 up to but not including 0.04 become white. All other pixels keep the reference exactly. A four-percent probability does not promise exactly four percent changed locations in one finite image. Some selected pixels could also already have an extreme value, so selection count and changed-value count are conceptually distinct. Inspect the mask beside the image to see which locations the simulation chose. A denoiser suitable for small Gaussian offsets may spread these extreme values into neighboring pixels, which is one reason to identify the disturbance before choosing a filter.

Try it

  1. Draw one seeded random array with the image’s height and width.
  2. Apply the two supplied disjoint replacement intervals to a reference copy.
  3. Display the corrupted image and selected-location mask.
Python · run in order
draws = np.random.default_rng(620).random(clean_rgb.shape[:2])
pepper = draws < 0.02
salt = (draws >= 0.02) & (draws < 0.04)
impulse_rgb = clean_rgb.copy()
impulse_rgb[pepper] = 0
impulse_rgb[salt] = 255
selected = pepper | salt
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(clean_rgb)
axes[0].set_title('Reference')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(impulse_rgb)
axes[1].set_title('Pixel replacements')
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[2].imshow(selected, cmap='gray', vmin=0, vmax=1)
axes[2].set_title('Selected locations')
axes[2].axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The mask shows the actual selected locations for this seed. Notice that most pixels remain untouched, unlike the additive disturbance in the previous task.

Change and compare

  • Check that no location belongs to both replacement masks.
  • Compare whole-pixel impulses with independently corrupting the three color channels.

Guided task 03

A normalized local averaging kernel

A local averaging filter replaces each value with a weighted combination of neighboring values. The three-by-three kernel here gives equal weight to nine positions and sums to one. On a constant region with a compatible border rule, that normalization preserves the constant value. It also mixes values across an edge, so reducing small local variation and softening fine detail are consequences of the same operation.

OpenCV filter2D uses the supplied kernel orientation as a correlation operation. For this symmetric averaging kernel, flipping it would make no difference, but that distinction matters for directional kernels later. The output depth is float32 so the calculation is not immediately rounded back to the original storage type. For display, values are clipped to zero through 255 and converted to uint8. The RGB array remains RGB; filtering does not secretly change the channel order. The reflected border policy supplies neighborhoods at the image boundary. Keep kernel normalization, output depth and border assumptions explicit when comparing filters.

Try it

  1. Use the Gaussian-corrupted image from teaching task 1.
  2. Apply a normalized three-by-three kernel with a reflected border and float output.
  3. Compare complete images and a crop containing fine printed lines.
Python · run in order
kernel = np.ones((3, 3), dtype='float32') / 9
box_float = cv2.filter2D(gaussian_rgb, cv2.CV_32F, kernel, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
box_rgb = np.clip(np.rint(box_float), 0, 255).astype('uint8')
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(gaussian_rgb)
axes[0].set_title('Noisy input')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(box_rgb)
axes[1].set_title('3x3 average')
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[2].imshow(gaussian_rgb[20:98, 10:73])
axes[2].set_title('Input detail')
axes[2].axis('off')
axes[3].imshow(box_rgb[20:98, 10:73])
axes[3].set_title('Averaged detail')
axes[3].axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Inspect the printed lines as well as the smooth desk surface. A quieter-looking surface does not establish that every task-relevant detail was preserved.

Change and compare

  • Use a five-by-five normalized kernel while keeping the noisy input unchanged.
  • Predict the output for a constant float image under the same reflected border.

Guided task 04

Gaussian scale and detail loss

Gaussian filtering assigns larger weights near the center of a neighborhood and smaller weights farther away. Kernel size limits the supported neighborhood, while sigma controls the spread of the weighting. Choose both explicitly for an interpretable experiment rather than relying on an implicit relationship that may be forgotten when the code is reused.

The two examples use the same noisy input and border policy but different spatial scales. A stronger blur can remove more short-scale variation, including both noise and genuine narrow lines. Compare the note text and book texture at equal display size. The weights do not know which fluctuations are accidental and which are important for a later classifier. In a future CNN pipeline, the decision to blur would need an evaluation that preserves independent data roles; prettier previews alone do not show better classification. Here the known reference and detail crops support an image-processing comparison only. Keep the unfiltered version available so preprocessing does not become an irreversible assumption.

Try it

  1. Filter the same noisy image with a 3x3, sigma 0.6 Gaussian and a 7x7, sigma 1.8 Gaussian.
  2. Use BORDER_REFLECT_101 in both cases.
  3. Compare the reference and both outputs at the same spatial scale.
Python · run in order
mild = cv2.GaussianBlur(gaussian_rgb, (3, 3), sigmaX=0.6, sigmaY=0.6, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
strong = cv2.GaussianBlur(gaussian_rgb, (7, 7), sigmaX=1.8, sigmaY=1.8, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(clean_rgb[18:124, 10:153])
axes[0].set_title('Reference detail')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(mild[18:124, 10:153])
axes[1].set_title('Sigma 0.6')
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[2].imshow(strong[18:124, 10:153])
axes[2].set_title('Sigma 1.8')
axes[2].axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Compare narrow marks and boundaries in both outputs. The stronger filter can remove variation that was part of the clean drawing, so visual smoothness is not the sole criterion.

Change and compare

  • Hold sigma fixed and change the kernel size to inspect truncation effects.
  • Identify a clean scene detail that could matter for a later recognition task.

Guided task 05

Median filtering for isolated extremes

A median filter chooses a middle value from the local ordered values rather than averaging them. An isolated extreme can therefore have little influence if enough neighboring values remain near the underlying signal. This makes a median operation a useful candidate for the sparse black-and-white replacements created earlier. It is nonlinear: the output is not a fixed weighted sum of the original pixels.

The comparison keeps the impulse-corrupted input fixed and applies a three-by-three median and a Gaussian filter. Inspect whether extreme specks remain, spread or disappear, while also checking small legitimate marks. Median filtering can remove genuine small objects or thin texture that resembles isolated corruption. Its RGB operation treats channels through their own local values, so do not assume it recognizes the original clean colors or object boundaries. OpenCV’s medianBlur uses a replicated border internally; it does not accept the same border argument as GaussianBlur. Parameter interfaces and border behavior belong in the comparison, especially when details near the image edge matter.

Try it

  1. Use the impulse-corrupted image from teaching task 2.
  2. Apply medianBlur with width three and a 3x3 Gaussian with sigma one.
  3. Compare their outputs with the same clean reference and corrupted input.
Python · run in order
median_rgb = cv2.medianBlur(impulse_rgb, 3)
impulse_gaussian = cv2.GaussianBlur(impulse_rgb, (3, 3), 1.0, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REPLICATE)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(clean_rgb)
axes[0].set_title('Reference')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(impulse_rgb)
axes[1].set_title('Impulse input')
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[2].imshow(median_rgb)
axes[2].set_title('3x3 median')
axes[2].axis('off')
axes[3].imshow(impulse_gaussian)
axes[3].set_title('3x3 Gaussian')
axes[3].axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Compare the neighborhood around a speck and around a real printed mark. A filter that removes an isolated impulse can also remove an equally small legitimate feature.

Change and compare

  • Test a five-by-five median while retaining the same corrupted image.
  • Explain why a middle-value rule cannot be represented by one fixed averaging kernel.

Guided task 06

Bilateral filtering uses value similarity

A bilateral filter combines spatial proximity with similarity of pixel values. Nearby pixels with very different values can receive less influence than equally nearby pixels with similar values. This can reduce variation inside regions while limiting some mixing across strong boundaries. It does not guarantee that every true edge or small texture survives, and it can leave or reshape certain artifacts.

The parameters have different units. Diameter limits the neighborhood, sigmaSpace describes spatial distance in pixels, and sigmaColor describes value differences in the current image scale. In this task the RGB array is uint8, so the color scale is zero through 255. Reusing the same numeric sigmaColor after converting the image to zero through one would describe a very different rule. Compare the bilateral result with a Gaussian result on the same noisy image, including a crop with both text and a broad surface. This is a controlled filter inspection, not evidence that one method universally prepares better CNN inputs.

Try it

  1. Apply bilateralFilter with diameter seven, sigmaColor twenty and sigmaSpace three.
  2. Create a 7x7 Gaussian comparison from the same noisy input.
  3. Inspect a common crop containing object boundaries and texture.
Python · run in order
bilateral = cv2.bilateralFilter(gaussian_rgb, d=7, sigmaColor=20, sigmaSpace=3, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
gaussian_compare = cv2.GaussianBlur(gaussian_rgb, (7, 7), 1.2, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(gaussian_rgb[20:104, 55:152])
axes[0].set_title('Noisy crop')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(gaussian_compare[20:104, 55:152])
axes[1].set_title('Gaussian crop')
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[2].imshow(bilateral[20:104, 55:152])
axes[2].set_title('Bilateral crop')
axes[2].axis('off')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Look for differences on both sides of boundaries and within smooth regions. The two filters use different weighting rules, so an appealing crop is not a general quality ranking.

Change and compare

  • Increase only sigmaColor and describe which neighbors gain influence.
  • State how the meaning of sigmaColor changes when pixel values are divided by 255.

Guided task 07

Border rules supply missing neighbors

A filter near the boundary asks for values outside the stored image. A border rule supplies those values. Constant-zero padding treats the missing region as black, while a reflected rule extends a mirrored pattern. These choices are assumptions, not observations of what was outside the camera frame or drawn canvas.

This task filters the clean image rather than a noisy one so the border effect is not confused with denoising. A five-by-five averaging kernel reaches two pixels beyond its center in each direction. With the same arithmetic and kernel, the interior region whose full neighborhood is present should agree between the two border rules. Differences are confined to the boundary band. A darkened outer strip under zero padding can be a processing artifact even if no such edge existed in the input. Cropping that strip later may remove the artifact, but it also changes the retained content. Record the chosen border policy instead of allowing an unnoticed default to define the pipeline.

Try it

  1. Filter the clean float image with the same 5x5 mean kernel under constant-zero and reflected borders.
  2. Compute their mean absolute channel difference.
  3. Inspect enlarged top-border crops and verify interior agreement.
Python · run in order
kernel = np.ones((5, 5), dtype='float32') / 25
constant = cv2.filter2D(clean_rgb.astype('float32'), -1, kernel, borderType=cv2.BORDER_CONSTANT)
reflected = cv2.filter2D(clean_rgb.astype('float32'), -1, kernel, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
border_difference = np.abs(constant - reflected).mean(axis=2)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 4, figsize=(16, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(clean_rgb[:18])
axes[0].set_title('Input top border')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(np.clip(constant[:18] / 255, 0, 1))
axes[1].set_title('Zero-border mean')
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[2].imshow(np.clip(reflected[:18] / 255, 0, 1))
axes[2].set_title('Reflected-border mean')
axes[2].axis('off')
error_image = axes[3].imshow(border_difference, cmap='magma', vmin=0, vmax=100)
axes[3].set_title('Border difference')
axes[3].axis('off')
fig.colorbar(error_image, ax=axes[3], label='Mean absolute channel difference')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

The difference map locates where the assumptions matter. Interior agreement is expected because those neighborhoods contain only stored pixels under either rule.

Change and compare

  • Predict the width of the affected band for a seven-by-seven kernel.
  • Check a constant-value test image to isolate border effects from scene texture.

Guided task 08

Known-reference error is a limited metric

Because the clean drawing is available, mean squared error can measure how far a candidate is from that reference. Compute differences in floating point, square them, and average over the stated pixels and channels. The resulting units are squared channel-value units on the zero-to-255 scale. Dividing both images by 255 first would change the numerical MSE scale, even though it would not change the ranking for those same candidates.

The metric treats every compared channel value equally. It can favor an output that loses a small but meaningful character if reducing widespread noise contributes more to the average. Inspect the reference, candidate and detail crops alongside the number. This task computes actual errors for the generated noisy image and one Gaussian-filtered version without requiring either to win. The clean reference exists only because this is a controlled simulation; a single real noisy image usually does not provide its own exact clean target. Most importantly, reconstruction MSE is not classifier accuracy. A later CNN experiment would need its own independent evaluation of the chosen preprocessing.

Try it

  1. Use the clean drawing, Gaussian-corrupted image and a stated Gaussian candidate.
  2. Calculate full-image MSE in floating point for both candidates.
  3. Display reference and candidate images beside the measured error bars.
Python · run in order
candidate = cv2.GaussianBlur(gaussian_rgb, (3, 3), 0.8, borderType=cv2.BORDER_REFLECT_101)
reference = clean_rgb.astype('float32')
mse_noisy = float(np.mean((gaussian_rgb.astype('float32') - reference) ** 2))
mse_candidate = float(np.mean((candidate.astype('float32') - reference) ** 2))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(12, 3.5))
axes[0].imshow(clean_rgb)
axes[0].set_title('Known reference')
axes[0].axis('off')
axes[1].imshow(candidate)
axes[1].set_title('Gaussian candidate')
axes[1].axis('off')
axes[2].bar(['Noisy', 'Candidate'], [mse_noisy, mse_candidate])
axes[2].set(ylabel='MSE in squared channel units', title='Actual reference error')
fig.tight_layout()

Read the result

Read the measured errors and inspect the image detail together. The code verifies finite arithmetic and the stated scale, not a universal improvement from filtering.

Change and compare

  • Measure only the printed-note crop and compare that question with whole-image MSE.
  • Explain why an image-reconstruction score cannot establish a CNN accuracy gain.
